analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses buried in consumer contracts for goods, services, and credit.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors backed it, the House Financial Services Committee referred it to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most standard consumer contracts — for credit cards, loans, phones, and other goods and services — include a clause requiring customers to give up their right to sue in court and instead resolve disputes before a private arbitrator chosen under the company's process, usually with no right to join a class action. This bill would make such clauses unenforceable and treat them as an unfair and deceptive trade practice. Companies could still use arbitration, but only if both sides agreed to it after a dispute actually arose.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with disputes against companies — such as borrowers, cardholders, and buyers of goods and services — who would keep their right to take a case to court, including through class actions, instead of being forced into private arbitration under terms the company wrote.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers disputing credit, goods, or services

how_it_helps.text: Would declare any pre-written arbitration clause in a consumer transaction or contract unenforceable and an unfair and deceptive trade practice under Federal or State law [S2] [S3].
Would still allow binding arbitration if both parties agree in writing after a controversy has already arisen, so voluntary arbitration remains available [S2] [S3].
Applies to all consumer transactions entered into after enactment, to future amendments to existing contracts, and to pending or later disputes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that write arbitration clauses into their standard consumer contracts — lenders, credit card issuers, and other sellers of goods and services — would face more lawsuits, including class actions, and lose a dispute process they control. Private arbitration providers would lose this stream of business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders and firms using arbitration clauses

drawbacks.text: The bill covers any individual in any consumer transaction, so the total volume of litigation against companies over small-dollar disputes would likely rise, and some of that cost could be passed to customers through prices or fees [S3].

Companies argue arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for many consumers; supporters of arbitration clauses contend bans benefit trial lawyers more than consumers, a cost an honest supporter would weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: forced arbitration clauses are typically accepted without real negotiation and can eliminate consumers' only practical remedy, especially class actions for small-dollar harms that no one would sue over individually. The cost is more litigation, some of it inefficient or passed on in prices. On balance the bill's protection of the right to sue outweighs the litigation cost, though the ban is broad in scope.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its subcommittee on financial institutions and consumer credit, and it never came back out for a vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez (D-IL) introduced the bill on April 30, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
On May 12, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit; no further action was recorded for the rest of the 108th Congress [S5].
The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and 5 Democratic cosponsors, and no committee vote, floor vote, or companion action is recorded [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that embed arbitration clauses in standard consumer contracts — lenders, credit card issuers, and other large sellers — kept the ability to route disputes into a process they write, and private arbitration providers kept the business. Consumers with grievances continued to face those clauses in their contracts.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the committee he sat on

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee, which took no action, keeping it from a committee vote or the floor for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Credit card and consumer lending industry
against.role: Companies whose standard contracts contained forced arbitration clauses
against.what_they_did: Relied on mandatory arbitration clauses across consumer credit contracts and opposed restricting them

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the bill died in committee without any recorded votes [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Consumer lenders and credit card issuers
industries.note: These companies write arbitration clauses into the standard contracts consumers sign to get credit. Striking the clauses would expose them to lawsuits, including class actions, that the clauses currently prevent; the consumer's loss of the right to sue is the company's gain under the status quo [S3].

Arbitration firms earn fees handling consumer disputes funneled to them by company-written clauses; the bill would cut off most of that consumer-dispute business, leaving only voluntary post-dispute agreements [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Consumer-facing businesses using standard-form contracts (telecom, retail, services)
industries.note: Firms across goods and services insert arbitration clauses in form contracts to avoid court; the bill would make those clauses unenforceable, and the right to sue it restores comes out of the firms' litigation exposure [S3].
